claim: G4C2 repeat expansions within the C9orf72 gene are the most common genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: G4C2 repeat expansions within the C9orf72 gene are the most common genetic cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: The G4C2 repeats undergo repeat-associated non-ATG translation to generate toxic dipeptide repeat proteins.
source: The repeats undergo repeat-associated non-ATG translation to generate toxic dipeptide repeat proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Insulin/IGF signalling is reduced in fly models of C9orf72 repeat expansion.
source: Here, we show that insulin/IGF signalling is reduced in fly models of C9orf72 repeat expansion using RNA sequencing of adult brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of insulin/IGF signalling can mitigate multiple neurodegenerative phenotypes in flies expressing either expanded G4C2 repeats or the toxic dipeptide repeat protein poly-GR.
source: We further demonstrate that activation of insulin/IGF signalling can mitigate multiple neurodegenerative phenotypes in flies expressing either expanded G4C2 repeats or the toxic dipeptide repeat protein poly-GR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fly models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Levels of poly-GR are reduced when components of the insulin/IGF signalling pathway are genetically activated in diseased flies.
source: Levels of poly-GR are reduced when components of the insulin/IGF signalling pathway are genetically activated in the diseased flies, suggesting a mechanism of rescue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of poly-GR levels in the manuscript.

claim: Modulating insulin signalling in mammalian cells lowers poly-GR levels.
source: Modulating insulin signalling in mammalian cells also lowers poly-GR levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mammalian cell culture experiments.

claim: Systemic injection of insulin improves the survival of flies expressing G4C2 repeats.
source: Remarkably, systemic injection of insulin improves the survival of flies expressing G4C2 repeats.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data from insulin injection experiments in flies.

claim: Modulation of insulin/IGF signalling could be an effective therapeutic approach against C9orf72 ALS/FTD.
source: Overall, our data suggest that modulation of insulin/IGF signalling could be an effective therapeutic approach against C9orf72 ALS/FTD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hexanucleotide G4C2 repeat expansion in the first intron of the C9orf72 gene is the most common genetic cause of ALS and FTD.
source: The most common genetic cause is a hexanucleotide G4C2 repeat expansion in the first intron of the C9orf72 gene (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011; Gijselinck et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Possible mechanisms for the expansion-related neurodegeneration include haploinsufficiency of the C9orf72 gene.
source: Possible mechanisms for the expansion-related neurodegeneration include (i) haploinsufficiency of the C9orf72 gene
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Possible mechanisms for the expansion-related neurodegeneration include transcription of the repeats in the sense and antisense direction with accumulation of RNA foci that sequester RNA binding proteins.
source: Possible mechanisms for the expansion-related neurodegeneration include (i) haploinsufficiency of the C9orf72 gene; (ii) transcription of the repeats in the sense and antisense direction with accumulation of RNA foci that sequester RNA binding proteins
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Possible mechanisms for the expansion-related neurodegeneration include production of toxic dipeptide-repeat proteins (DPRs) through repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation.
source: Possible mechanisms for the expansion-related neurodegeneration include (i) haploinsufficiency of the C9orf72 gene; (ii) transcription of the repeats in the sense and antisense direction with accumulation of RNA foci that sequester RNA binding proteins; (iii) production of toxic dipeptide-repeat proteins (DPRs) through repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation (Gijselinck et al., 2012; Balendra and Isaacs, 2018; Zu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Five DPRs are produced: poly-GA, poly-GR, poly-GP, poly-PA, and poly-PR.
source: From the five DPRs produced (poly-GA, poly-GR, poly-GP, poly-PA, and poly-PR)
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The arginine-containing dipeptides poly-GR and poly-PR are highly toxic in cell lines, cultured neurons, Drosophila, and mice.
source: From the five DPRs produced (poly-GA, poly-GR, poly-GP, poly-PA, and poly-PR), the arginine-containing dipeptides poly-GR and poly-PR are highly toxic in cell lines, cultured neurons, Drosophila, and mice (Mizielinska et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018b; Zhang et al., 2019; Moens et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Several mechanisms contribute to DPR-induced toxicity, including impaired translation, nucleolar stress, DNA damage, impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport, and altered stress granule dynamics.
source: Several mechanisms contribute to DPR-induced toxicity, including impaired translation, nucleolar stress, DNA damage, impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport, and altered stress granule dynamics (Kwon et al., 2014; Freibaum et al., 2015; Jovičić et al., 2015; Kanekura et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Boeynaems et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018a; Moens et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signals through a highly conserved pathway that regulates a multitude of processes such as protein synthesis, cell growth, and cell differentiation in both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signals through a highly conserved pathway that regulates a multitude of processes such as protein synthesis, cell growth, and cell differentiation in both vertebrates and invertebrates (Barbieri et al., 2003; Broughton and Partridge, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In vertebrates, insulin and IGFs are subspecialized into systems with overlapping but distinct biological functions.
source: In vertebrates, insulin and IGFs are subspecialized into systems with overlapping but distinct biological functions
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In invertebrates there is a single insulin-like system that has the dual function of insulin/IGF signalling.
source: while in invertebrates there is a single insulin-like system that has the dual function of insulin/IGF signalling.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activation of the insulin receptor (InR)/IGF-1 receptor through binding insulin/IGF-1 triggers the recruitment of an insulin receptor substrate, which in turn activates PI3-kinase and subsequently 3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1 (PDK1).
source: Activation of the insulin receptor (InR)/IGF-1 receptor through binding insulin/IGF-1 triggers the recruitment of an insulin receptor substrate, which in turn activates PI3-kinase and subsequently 3-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1 (PDK1).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of insulin signaling pathways.

claim: PDK1 can regulate translation via Akt and S6K.
source: PDK1 can regulate translation via Akt and S6K.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of insulin signaling pathways.

claim: PDK1 activates Akt, which then activates mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR).
source: PDK1 activates Akt, which then activates mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR)
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of insulin signaling pathways.

claim: mTOR phosphorylates translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein (4E-BP), subsequently releasing its inhibition of the translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E).
source: which phosphorylates translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein (4E-BP), subsequently releasing its inhibition of the translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of insulin signaling pathways.

claim: PDK1 can activate translation initiation factor 4B (eIF4B) through ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) phosphorylation.
source: PDK1 can also activate translation initiation factor 4B (eIF4B) through ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of insulin signaling pathways.

claim: Translation initiation is increased, protein synthesis is up-regulated, and the proteostatic machinery is also up-regulated as a consequence of insulin signaling activation.
source: Consequently, translation initiation is increased, protein synthesis is up-regulated, and the proteostatic machinery is also up-regulated (Brogiolo et al., 2001; Wullschleger et al., 2006; Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Martina et al., 2012; Minard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: IGF-1 is an important neurotrophin for the maintenance and survival of motor neurons.
source: IGF-1 is an important neurotrophin for the maintenance and survival of motor neurons
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In vivo studies in mouse models of SOD1-ALS have suggested that IGF-1 and IGF-2 have therapeutic efficacy.
source: and in vivo studies in mouse models of SOD1-ALS have suggested that IGF-1 and IGF-2 have therapeutic efficacy (Kaspar et al., 2003; Allodi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The connection between insulin/IGF signalling and C9ALS/FTD is not yet clear.
source: However, the connection between insulin/IGF signalling and C9ALS/FTD is not yet clear.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: Expression of (G4C2)36 in adult Drosophila neurons leads to a decrease in the levels of the insulin receptor ligands dilp2, dilp3, and dilp5.
source: Here, we present evidence that expression of (G4C2)36 in adult Drosophila neurons leads to a decrease in the levels of the insulin receptor ligands dilp2, dilp3, and dilp5.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Over-expression of an active form of the single fly insulin/IGF receptor InR in neurons partially rescued the toxicity associated with poly-GR expression in C9orf72 repeat fly models.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of an active form of the single fly insulin/IGF receptor InR in neurons, or insulin treatment, partially rescued the toxicity associated with poly-GR expression in C9orf72 repeat fly models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fly models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Insulin treatment partially rescued the toxicity associated with poly-GR expression in C9orf72 repeat fly models.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of an active form of the single fly insulin/IGF receptor InR in neurons, or insulin treatment, partially rescued the toxicity associated with poly-GR expression in C9orf72 repeat fly models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fly models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased insulin/IGF signalling lowered the level of poly-GR in both fly neurons and mammalian cells.
source: Increased insulin/IGF signalling lowered the level of poly-GR in both fly neurons and mammalian cells, identifying a mechanism of rescue of poly-GR toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both fly and mammalian cell experiments.

claim: Enhanced insulin/IGF signalling may provide a potential therapeutic target to ameliorate the toxic effects of the C9orf72 repeat expansion.
source: Our findings indicate that enhanced insulin/IGF signalling may provide a potential therapeutic target to ameliorate the toxic effects of the C9orf72 repeat expansion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: RNA-seq was performed on heads of adult flies expressing ATG-driven GR100 specifically in neurons, using the Elav-GS RU486-inducible driver.
source: To identify disease-specific gene expression patterns associated with poly-GR, we performed RNA-seq on heads of adult flies expressing ATG-driven GR100 specifically in neurons, using the Elav-GS RU486-inducible driver.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: RNA-seq was performed three days after induction of GR100 expression, in order to identify early changes prior to overt neurodegeneration.
source: RNA-seq was performed three days after induction of GR100 expression, in order to identify early changes prior to overt neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Flies expressing poly-GR100 showed strong alterations in their transcriptome when compared with the control line.
source: These flies showed strong alterations in their transcriptome when compared with the control line.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 2754 genes were significantly differentially regulated (adjusted p<0.05) in flies expressing poly-GR100.
source: We identified 2754 genes significantly differentially regulated (adjusted p<0.05) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and GEO: GSE151826).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Flies expressing poly-GR100 showed altered expression of genes involved in pathways previously implicated in C9orf72 pathology, including translation, DNA damage and repair, proteasome, and RNA metabolism.
source: Flies expressing poly-GR100 showed altered expression of genes involved in pathways previously implicated in C9orf72 pathology, including translation, DNA damage and repair, proteasome, and RNA metabolism (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neuropeptide hormone activity was the most enriched category of down-regulated genes in flies expressing poly-GR100.
source: Interestingly, neuropeptide hormone activity was the most enriched category of down-regulated genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (dilps) 2, 3, and 5 were highly down-regulated in flies expressing poly-GR100 (3.7-, 9.5-, and 3.2-fold change, respectively), adjusted p value<0.05.
source: Among these neuropeptides, Drosophila insulin-like peptides (dilps) 2, 3, and 5 were highly down-regulated (3.7-, 9.5-, and 3.2-fold change, respectively), adjusted p value<0.05 – Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RT-PCR analysis of brains of flies expressing poly-GR confirmed the lowered expression of dilp 2, 3, and 5.
source: RT-PCR analysis of brains of flies expressing poly-GR confirmed the lowered expression of dilp 2, 3, and 5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lower expression of dilps was observed in flies expressing (G4C2)36, although the expression change in the dilp5 gene did not reach statistical significance.
source: To test whether these dilps were also down-regulated in a GGGGCC repeat model that generates poly-GR via RAN translation, we performed RT-PCR in flies expressing (G4C2)36. Lower expression of dilps was also observed in this model, although the expression change in the dilp5 gene did not reach statistical significance (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dilps 2, 3, and 5 are neuropeptides secreted by insulin-producing cells (IPCs) in the Drosophila brain.
source: Dilps 2, 3, and 5 are neuropeptides secreted by insulin-producing cells (IPCs) in the Drosophila brain (Brogiolo et al., 2001; Ikeya et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Dilp2 immunostaining showed no alteration in the number of IPCs in flies expressing poly-GR in all neurons.
source: To investigate whether reduced expression of dilps was simply due to the death of IPCs, we imaged brains of flies expressing poly-GR in all neurons. Dilp2 immunostaining showed no alteration in the number of IPCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Dilp2 protein levels were reduced in IPCs expressing poly-GR.
source: However, consistent with our RNA-seq data, Dilp2 protein levels were reduced in IPCs expressing poly-GR (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Expression of poly-GR specifically in IPCs using the dilp3-Gal4 driver was not sufficient to induce neuronal cell death.
source: In addition, expression of poly-GR specifically in IPCs using the dilp3-Gal4 driver was not sufficient to induce neuronal cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Reduction of dilp2, dilp3, and dilp5 expression in GR100 flies was not due to loss of IPCs.
source: Reduction of dilp2, dilp3, and dilp5 expression in GR100 flies was therefore not due to loss of IPCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunostaining data showing no loss of IPCs.

claim: Dilps signal via a single insulin/IGF receptor (InR), through which they regulate the main signalling pathways that modulate 4E-BP1 phosphorylation.
source: Dilps signal via a single insulin/IGF receptor (InR), through which they regulate the main signalling pathways that modulate 4E-BP1 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), a well-described read-out of insulin signalling in Drosophila (Bhandari et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2003; Blancquaert et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research and referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Flies expressing (G4C2)36 had significantly decreased ratio of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 to the non-phosphorylated form, indicative of reduced insulin signalling.
source: To assess insulin/IGF pathway activity, we measured the phosphorylation state of 4E-BP1 in (G4C2)36 flies, and found that they had significantly decreased ratio of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 to the non-phosphorylated form, indicative of reduced insulin signalling (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Co-expressing a constitutively active insulin receptor (InRActive) significantly increased the ratio of phosphorylated 4E-BP1 to the non-phosphorylated form, indicating a rescue of insulin/IGF signalling immediately downstream of the dilps.
source: Co-expressing a constitutively active insulin receptor (InRActive) significantly increased this ratio, indicating a rescue of insulin/IGF signalling immediately downstream of the dilps (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: There is a reduction in insulin/IGF pathway activity in flies expressing either G4C2 repeats or poly-GR as a result of a reduction in expression of the dilps.
source: Taken together, these data indicate a reduction in insulin/IGF pathway activity in flies expressing either G4C2 repeats or poly-GR as a result of a reduction in expression of the dilps.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data on dilp expression and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation.

claim: The lifespan of flies co-expressing (G4C2)36 and InRActive specifically in neurons was significantly extended (p<0.001).
source: To assess this, we monitored the survival of flies co-expressing (G4C2)36 and InRActive, specifically in neurons, and found that their lifespan was significantly extended (p<0.001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Reducing insulin signalling through the expression of dominant-negative InR (InRDN) significantly reduced lifespan (p=0.027) in flies expressing (G4C2)36.
source: In contrast, reducing insulin signalling through the expression of dominant-negative InR (InRDN) significantly reduced lifespan (p=0.027) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activating insulin signalling in neurons reduced lifespan of wild-type flies (InRActivep<0.0001).
source: Activating insulin signalling in neurons reduced lifespan of wild-type flies (InRActivep<0.0001), as previously reported (Ismail et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data and a citation to published research.

claim: Reduction of insulin signalling led to increased lifespan (p=0.035) in wild-type flies.
source: whilst its reduction led to increased lifespan (p=0.035) (Figure 2B), again as previously reported (Augustin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to published research.

claim: Increasing insulin/IGF signalling specifically suppresses C9orf72 repeat toxicity.
source: These observations indicate that increasing insulin/IGF signalling specifically suppresses C9orf72 repeat toxicity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lifespan data showing differential effects in disease vs. wild-type flies.

claim: There was no significant difference between the amount of food ingested across the different experimental groups expressing (G4C2)36 with or without InR constructs.
source: To exclude the possibility that the rescue effect was a consequence of decreased fly feeding, and therefore reduced induction of the (G4C2)36 transgene, we measured food intake. There was no significant difference between the amount ingested across the different experimental groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neither expression of InRActive or InRDN altered the G4C2 transcript levels.
source: To rule out the possibility that expression of either InRActive or InRDN had a direct effect on the transcription of the G4C2 transgene, we measured the transcript repeat levels by RNA dot blot analysis in flies ubiquitously expressing the two constructs. Neither expression of InRActive or InRDN altered the G4C2 transcript levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA dot blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP levels were unaltered in neuronal cells expressing InRActive or InRDN.
source: To further investigate whether expression of InRActive or InRDN indirectly affected the inducible protein expression system, we measured levels of GFP driven by the Elav-GS RU486-inducible driver and found that they were unaltered in neuronal cells expressing InRActive or InRDN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Activation of insulin/IGF signalling ameliorated C9orf72 repeat toxicity, rather than simply reducing expression of the (G4C2)36 transgene.
source: Activation of insulin/IGF signalling therefore ameliorated C9orf72 repeat toxicity, rather than simply reducing expression of the (G4C2)36 transgene.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the control experiments showing no effect on transgene expression.

claim: Flies expressing (G4C2)36 in adult neurons exhibited decreased locomotor activity (p=0.0003).
source: To confirm that increasing insulin signalling could also ameliorate a second, distinct (G4C2)36-induced neuronal phenotype, we recorded motor activity and day sleep using a Drosophila activity monitor system. Flies expressing (G4C2)36 in adult neurons exhibited decreased locomotor activity (p=0.0003)
evidence: This claim is supported by activity monitoring data.

claim: Flies expressing (G4C2)36 in adult neurons exhibited extended sleep periods during the day and night.
source: Flies expressing (G4C2)36 in adult neurons exhibited decreased locomotor activity (p=0.0003) and extended sleep periods during the day and night (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E)
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The decreased locomotor activity and extended sleep phenotypes in flies expressing (G4C2)36 were abolished by expression of InRActive.
source: and these phenotypes were abolished by expression of InRActive (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by activity and sleep monitoring data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Increased levels of p53 have been observed in C9orf72 patient iPSC-neurons and fly models.
source: Increased levels of p53 have been observed in C9orf72 patient iPSC-neurons and fly models, and have been suggested to be a downstream marker of repeat-induced toxicity (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Co-expression of InRactive in (G4C2)36 flies led to a significant reduction in p53 levels.
source: We therefore tested if co-expression of InRactive in (G4C2)36 flies was associated with decreased levels of p53 and found that it led to a significant reduction (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No difference in p53 levels was observed in uninduced flies expressing (G4C2)36 and InRactive.
source: whereas no difference was observed in uninduced flies (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Increased insulin/IGF signalling can ameliorate multiple read-outs of G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity.
source: These results show that increased insulin/IGF signalling can ameliorate multiple read-outs of G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data on lifespan, activity, sleep, and p53 levels.

claim: Toxicity in the (G4C2)36 flies is mediated by poly-GR.
source: As toxicity in the (G4C2)36 flies is mediated by poly-GR (Mizielinska et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Increased p53 has been suggested to be driven by poly-GR.
source: and increased p53 has been suggested to be driven by poly-GR (Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2016Lopez-Gonzalez et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Ectopic expression of GR36 resulted in a mild rough eye and decreased eye size.
source: As previously reported (Mizielinska et al., 2014), ectopic expression of GR36 resulted in a mild rough eye and decreased eye size (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye phenotype data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to published research.

claim: Co-expression of GR36 with InRActive increased the size and decreased the roughness of the eyes.
source: Co-expression of GR36 with InRActive increased the size and decreased the roughness of the eyes
evidence: This claim is supported by eye phenotype data.

claim: Co-expression of GR36 with InRDN exacerbated the rough eye phenotype and further decreased eye size.
source: whereas co-expression with InRDN exacerbated the rough eye phenotype and further decreased eye size (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye phenotype data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of insulin/IGF signalling on eye size in diseased flies was much larger than in flies not expressing the dipeptide repeats (p<0.0001, two-way ANOVA), indicating a specific additional interaction of insulin signalling with C9orf72 repeat-induced toxicity.
source: Although insulin/IGF signalling also influenced eye cell growth in flies not expressing the dipeptide repeats (Figure 3B), the effect in diseased flies was much larger (p<0.0001, two-way ANOVA), indicating a specific additional interaction of insulin signalling with C9orf72 repeat-induced toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye phenotype data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of dilp2 had no effect on the eye phenotype of GR36 flies.
source: Expression of dilp2 had no effect (Figure 3C), likely because of a negative feedback system that acts to coordinate Dilp expression levels in the central nervous system (Grönke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye phenotype data shown in Figure 3C and a citation to published research.

claim: Over-expression of activated PI3K partially rescued the eye size of GR36 flies.
source: We co-expressed GR36 with activated PI3K or Akt, which function downstream of the InR, and found that over-expression of either partially rescued the eye size of GR36 flies (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye phenotype data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Over-expression of activated Akt partially rescued the eye size of GR36 flies.
source: We co-expressed GR36 with activated PI3K or Akt, which function downstream of the InR, and found that over-expression of either partially rescued the eye size of GR36 flies (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye phenotype data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Increased insulin/IGF signalling through the InR/PI3K/Akt pathway can rescue neurotoxicity associated with poly-GR expression.
source: Together, these observations show that increased insulin/IGF signalling through the InR/PI3K/Akt pathway can rescue neurotoxicity associated with poly-GR expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the eye phenotype rescue experiments.

claim: Expression of InRActive significantly decreased poly-GR levels in flies expressing (G4C2)36.
source: Using a quantitative Meso Scale Discovery (MSD) immunoassay, we found that expression of InRActive significantly decreased poly-GR levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MSD immunoassay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neuronal expression of InRActive in GR100-expressing flies reduced poly-GR levels.
source: In order to investigate whether the effect of InRActive on poly-GR levels occurs at the level of RAN translation, we investigated whether InRActive could reduce poly-GR levels in GR100 expressing flies, which generate poly-GR but do not undergo RAN translation. Neuronal expression of InRActive in GR100-expressing flies reduced poly-GR levels (Figure 4B)
evidence: This claim is supported by MSD immunoassay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neuronal expression of InRActive in GR100-expressing flies resulted in a concomitant extension of lifespan.
source: with a concomitant extension of lifespan (Figure 4C)
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: InRActive is acting downstream of RAN translation to reduce poly-GR levels.
source: This indicates that InRActive is acting downstream of RAN translation to reduce poly-GR levels
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that InRActive reduces poly-GR levels in GR100 flies which do not undergo RAN translation.

claim: Insulin/IGF signalling activation ameliorates toxicity by decreasing poly-GR levels.
source: and suggests that insulin/IGF signalling activation ameliorates toxicity by decreasing poly-GR levels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data showing reduced poly-GR levels and improved phenotypes with InRActive expression.

claim: MK2206 (pan-Akt inhibitor) increased NLuc/polyGR levels (1.77-fold ± 0.54 SD, p=0.0168) in HEK293T cells.
source: MK2206 increased NLuc/polyGR levels (1.77-fold ± 0.54 SD, p=0.0168) (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by nanoluciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SF1670 (PTEN inhibitor) decreased NLuc/polyGR levels (0.24-fold ± 0.09 SD, p=0.041) in HEK293T cells.
source: while SF1670 decreased NLuc/polyGR levels (0.24-fold ± 0.09 SD, p=0.041) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nanoluciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increasing insulin signalling via Akt decreased poly-GR levels in mammalian cells, while inhibiting the pathway increased poly-GR.
source: Therefore, consistent with our data in flies, increasing insulin signalling via Akt decreased poly-GR levels, while inhibiting the pathway increased poly-GR.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mammalian cell culture experiments with MK2206 and SF1670.

claim: Insulin treatment (0.03 mg/ml) significantly extended lifespan in three independent cohorts of flies expressing (G4C2)36.
source: We injected 0.03 mg/ml insulin into fly haemolymph, equivalent to blood, at the second and seventh day post-induction of (G4C2)36 expression, and determined the effect on fly survival. Insulin treatment significantly extended lifespan in three independent cohorts of flies (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Insulin treatment modestly reduced lifespan in control, uninduced flies.
source: while modestly reducing lifespan in control, uninduced flies, again indicating a beneficial effect of insulin signalling specific to C9orf72 repeat toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data.

claim: Higher concentrations of insulin became toxic.
source: Higher concentrations of insulin became toxic (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), indicating there is a therapeutic window within which insulin treatment is beneficial.
